articles.title: Second Philippine exporter ships Carabao mangoes to Canada
articles.summary: Weekly shipments are planned as exporters build a larger Canadian market.

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 6:14pm
Stock photo of Philippine mangoes sold at a market.
Wikimedia Commons

MANILA, Philippines — A second Philippine exporter has begun shipping Carabao mangoes to Canada, flying one metric ton to Vancouver as the government looks for new overseas buyers for the iconic sweet fruit.
The 250 cartons from Mensch FilAm Corp. were flown to Vancouver on September 18 and are bound for Vancouver distributor Fresh Makers Ltd., the Department of Agriculture said Monday, September 21.
The cargo adds a second supply line into Canada after the first-ever shipment of Carabao mangoes in June.

The export of Carabao mangoes first entered the Canadian market in June, when the DA sent off 1 metric ton to Toronto supplied by Hi-Las Marketing Corp. and Castillo Import Export Ventures Inc. and imported by Ontario-based TSI Tropicals Inc.
That supply chain delivered 100 cases to T&T Supermarket in the Vancouver area on September 9, according to the Philippine Consulate General in Vancouver.

The consulate said Mensch FilAm is the second major exporter supplying the Canadian market and shipments would arrive weekly at retailers and Asian supermarkets in Greater Vancouver and the Pacific region, with distribution to central and eastern Canada to follow.
Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said the shipment is part of a wider government effort to open new markets for Philippine farm products and raise agricultural export earnings.
State of Carabao mango exports
Most Carabao mangoes are sold at home.

The country produced about 710,000 metric tons of mangoes in 2025, and about 92% of the fruit is consumed locally, with the rest exported mainly to Hong Kong, South Korea and Japan, according to the Department of Science and Technology's Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development (DOST-PCAARRD), citing Philippine Statistics Authority data.
Canada is one of several new markets the government has pursued for the Carabao mango. In June 2025, the DA announced the first commercial shipment of Philippine mangoes to Italy.

articles.title: Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows
articles.summary:
Chancellor acknowledges disastrous state election results but vow to push on is likely to further alienate voters, and his own party

•

blocks.text: Friedrich Merz called it a “disaster”, and that was even before the full scale of the catastrophe for himself and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came into view after Sunday’s state elections.

In what one outlet called a “power move”, the German chancellor made a highly unusual televised speech just minutes after polls closed in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, attempting to get ahead of the narrative with a pledge to stay on and fight for his economic recovery programme.

But as the results trickled in, it became apparent that the CDU had not only scored its worst-ever result in a state election, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it had crashed out of a regional parliament altogether for the first time in postwar history with just 4.9% of the vote in the region on the Baltic coast.
The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came out on top for the third time in a German state, drawing 38% against 35.5% for the centre-left Social Democrats, Merz’s federal coalition partner.

Although the AfD has little chance of taking power because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties, the anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly party could celebrate a further success in destabilising the German political establishment.

In Berlin, the CDU will almost certainly have to vacate city hall once the coalition negotiations wrap up after a stinging defeat to the leftwing Linke party, which is calling for the expropriation of corporate landlords to address a housing crisis.

Polls had been predicting the humiliating result for Merz’s conservatives, which came after a historic rout two weeks ago in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the CDU scored just 17% to the AfD’s nearly 44%.

But the cumulative effect of these losses, coupled with Merz’s dire approval ratings and a far right with clear momentum, can hardly be exaggerated. Despite his vow to stay the course, many regard the German leader to be on borrowed time.

“Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival,” said the Berenberg bank’s chief economist, Holger Schmieding. “Although Merz has vowed to stay on as chancellor to spearhead the much needed pro-growth reforms, it will not be easy for him to contain the unrest within his party.”

Speculation was already rife after the Saxony-Anhalt race about a Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap. But as long as none of the potential successors appears ready to wield the dagger, and Merz remains unwilling to step aside, a volatile deadlock will reign.
after newsletter promotion
Merz, 70, gathered the CDU leadership at the party headquarters in Berlin to watch the exit polls together late on Sunday.

Local media reported that some of those assembled loudly objected to the defiant, full-steam-ahead speech he planned to deliver regarding his programme, saying that it amounted to ignoring what voters were shouting from the rooftops with their choices.
Merz cancelled a planned trip to New York this week to speak before the UN general assembly, already anticipating he would need to be in Berlin to grapple with the state elections’ aftermath.
Now, more than ever, he will have his work cut out for him after just 16 months in office.

articles.title: Tree vaccines and gene-edited butterflies among biotechnology projects funded by UK ‘invention agency’
articles.summary:
Exclusive: The tax-funded research aims to protect British wildlife from the human-caused climate crisis

Vaccines for ash trees, skin treatments for newts and gene-edited swallowtail…

blocks.text: Vaccines for ash trees, skin treatments for newts and gene-edited swallowtail butterflies are among 14 tax-funded projects from the UK’s “invention agency” aiming to accelerate nature’s ability to adapt to the climate crisis.

The £54m accelerated adaptation programme from the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria) – a public body that funds high-risk, high-reward tech projects – aims to investigate applications of biotechnology that can speed up wild species’ evolution and help them to adapt to new threats such as global warming and disease.

The 14 teams announced on Monday will receive a share of an initial £30m in grants over the next two years. They will develop tools to protect native British wildlife species, including the English oak tree and critical pollinators such as the buff-tailed bumblebee, said Yannick Wurm, the director of the accelerated adaptation programme at Aria.

blocks.caption: A buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) on Marlborough Downs in Wiltshire, England. Photograph: Nick Upton/Alamy

blocks.text: The world’s natural environments are changing so rapidly owing to the climate crisis and human pressures that many species can no longer adapt quickly enough, said Wurm, a professor of evolutionary genomics at Queen Mary University, London. “This cohort is a first exploration of how we can harness some of the powers of biotechnology to responsibly help wild animals and plants to overcome challenges they face,” he added.

The projects aim to work alongside conventional nature conservation measures, such as protected reserves, to give environmentalists a new set of “precision tools” that Wurm compares to mRNA vaccines for humans.
Aria is the brainchild of Dominic Cummings, the former chief adviser to Boris Johnson, who said it would fund “crazy” ideas that could “restore Britain’s place as a scientific superpower”.

The publicly funded body has attracted criticism for its research into controversial geoengineering techniques and grants that have given millions in UK taxpayer money to US tech companies and venture capital firms. Matt Clifford, Aria’s chair, was forced to stand down this month over what one senior MP called a “clear conflict of interest” after taking a job with Anthropic, the developer of the AI chatbot Claude.

One team announced on Monday, led by researchers at the University of Exeter, will use Crispr-Cas9 gene-editing on the swallowtail, a butterfly on Britain’s red list of endangered species, to increase its resistance to insecticides used widely on farms. Another project developed by Rothamsted Research, the 180-year-old agricultural research facility in Hertfordshire, will edit the genes of long-lived tree species such as oaks to reproduce in months rather than decades, meaning they can rapidly develop adaptive responses to drought and invasive pathogens.

Environmentalists across the planet have debated using increasingly powerful biotechnology and gene-editing techniques to aid conservation. At the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s (IUCN) world conservation congress last October, more than 90 NGOs raised concerns that these technologies will irreversibly alter natural systems with unpredictable effects.

The ban was narrowly rejected after 250 scientists signed an open letter to highlight the potential benefits of synthetic biology, which could allow small islands to eliminate invasive mice that threaten more than 100 birds and reptiles. Instead, the IUCN adopted its first global policy on synthetic biology, including a set of stringent criteria for proposed solutions.

This IUCN policy has been one foundation of Aria’s ethical policy, said Marie-Claire Cordonier Segger, the chair of the programme’s ethical and social responsibility advisory committee. Although the projects are intended for the wild, none of the experimental solutions will be released during the programme, which will last until 2030, said Cordonier Segger, a professor of international law at the University of Cambridge. “The decision was made early to have the strongest possible code,” she said, adding that all grantees will work in secure labs.

Chris Thomas, founding director of the Leverhulme Centre for Anthropocene Biodiversity at the University of York, said the projects that Aria is funding offer potentially valuable tools at a time when many species and ecosystems face drought, pathogens and other threats.

Skin-eating chytrid fungal infections, which have caused population declines in more than 500 amphibian species, seems a “particularly worthy target” for these new approaches, said Thomas, who is not involved in the Aria programme.
after newsletter promotion

Biologists have so far had few options to prevent the spread in the wild, leading the Boston-based research lab Cultivarium to propose their project in partnership with Imperial College and Queen Mary University, London. It would genetically engineer a bacteria that lives on amphibians’ skin to produce proteins that “bind and stop” the infection, said Henry Lee, Cultivarium’s co-founder. “We’re not genetically engineering the amphibian; rather what we’re trying to do is we’re trying to give them a shield,” he said.

blocks.caption: Symptoms of ash dieback on a young ash coppice in Wayland Wood, Norfolk. Scientists at Aria believe they can give the trees a ‘vaccination’ against the disease. Photograph: David Mark/Alamy

blocks.text: Another project aims to prevent ash dieback – a fungal disease that is expected to kill half of Britain’s ash trees – by injecting the tree with RNA molecules that interfere with the fungus’s ability to infect. “So it is like giving the tree a vaccination,” said project lead Sarah Christofides, a mycologist at Cardiff University.

But Thomas cautions that the impact of these solutions will probably be “modest” and difficult to assess. While 90 amphibian species have gone extinct owing to chytrid infection, others show signs of adaptive resistance, he said. Making certain species within a pond more resistant will inevitably affect the species not targeted, he added.

To think that these interventions have an important role to play in preventing biodiversity loss “is probably pretty naive”, he said. To be deployed in the field, solutions will not only have to prove they are effective in the lab but win approval from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which has tightly controlled the releases of genetically modified organisms.
A further £24m will be allotted to projects that have shown success over the initial two years. Wurm said he hoped that a handful of successes would be “world-changing”.
Ultimately, our “most urgent challenge” is to halt and reverse human-controlled drivers of environmental change, he said, but these projects aim to offer solutions in the places where we cannot.

MANILA, Philippines – Carlos Yulo gave himself three chances to win perhaps the only medal missing in his collection as he advanced to three apparatus finals in the men’s artistic gymnastics of the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

Yulo, a double Olympic gold medalist and a multi-time world champion, reached the medal round of the floor exercise, vault, and parallel bars following a solid showing in the qualifications at the Nagoya General Gymnasium on Monday, September 21.

Living up to his billing as one of the Philippines’ best gold-medal bets in the continental showpiece, Yulo emerged as the top qualifier in the floor exercise, where he posted 14.6 points to edge South Korea’s Ryu Sung-hyun (14.566) and Japan’s Shoma Tsukiyama (14.166).

Yulo, though, almost failed to make the cut in his other pet event, finishing seventh in vault — an apparatus where he won two world titles — and doing just enough to earn a spot in the eight-man final.
A missed landing in his first vault netted Yulo only 13.166 points, but he redeemed himself with 14.133 points in his second vault for a 13.649 average.
While the qualifications might have been a mixed bag, Yulo views it as a lesson learned.
“There were a lot of learnings that I can use in the coming days,” Yulo said in Filipino.

Yulo also made the final of parallel bars, where he wound up as the fifth-best qualifier with 14.266 points, behind China’s Zou Jingyuan (15.333) and Zhang Boheng (14.7), Japan’s Shinnosuke Oka (14.633), and Tomoharu Tsunogai (14.633).
Japanese star Daiki Hashimoto also finished ahead of Yulo with 14.3 points, but he got the boot as only two gymnasts per country advance to each apparatus final.
Aside from Yulo, his younger brother Eldrew and Juancho Miguel Besana clinched final berths.
Eldrew landed fourth in the floor exercise (13.966) and finished as the seventh-best qualifier in horizontal bar (13.433), while Besana placed fourth in vault with 13.933 points.
In the individual all-around, Eldrew ended up as the best Filipino, getting seventh with 77.264 points followed by Carlos (75.465) at ninth and Besana (70.898).
Zhang captured the individual all-around gold with 85.065 points, besting Oka (84.698) and Hashimoto (83.865)
Meanwhile, the Philippines — also represented by Justine Ace de Leon and Zachary Nunez — qualified for the men’s team final as the sixth-best squad with 232.093 points.
The men’s team final is set on Wednesday, September 23, while the apparatus finals are scheduled on Thursday, September 24, and Friday, September 25. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte remained company director even after assuming VP post -- witness
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte remained one of the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President, a witness from…

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:56pm

Vice President Sara Duterte remained one of the Board of Directors of Metro City Chow Foods Corporation until 2025 or even after she was elected and assumed office as Vice President, a witness from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) said Monday.

SEC Company Registration and Monitoring Department Director Gerardo Fernando del Rosario made the testimony during Day 27 of the impeachment trial of Duterte, saying the Vice President’s position in the said firm was reflected on Metro City Chow Foods Corporation submissions to the SEC.
“Ayon po sa GIS nila from 2022-2024, si VP Sara Duterte ay member pa rin po ng Board of Directors,” Del Rosario said, referring to General Information Sheet.
(Based on its GIS from 2022 to 2024, Vice President Duterte is a member of the Board of Directors [of Metro City Chow Foods Corp.)
Asked about the following year’s filing, the SEC official confirmed: “Member pa rin siya ng Board of Directors sa GIS ng 2025.”
(The GIS of the same firm showed the Vice President remained as one of the Board of Directors in year 2025.)

Asked by private prosecutor Erwin Matib to explain what a board does, Del Rosario described its authority over the corporation’s business and property, as well as its responsibilities to shareholders and government agencies.
On the board’s role in conducting the company’s business, Del Rosario replied, “Hindi po siya makakapag-conduct ng business kung wala po siyang Board of Directors.”
(A firm cannot conduct business without a Board of Directors.)
Prohibited under 1987 Constitution
Also on Monday, Del Rosario said the Constitution prohibits the Vice President from participating in any business as provided under Article 7, Section 13 of the Constitution.

During the same hearing, Del Rosario said that GenCorp. Industries Inc. (GenCorp), a firm declared by Vice President Duterte as one of her business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), did not list her as an incorporator or director based on the firm’s General Information Sheet and Audited Financial Statement submitted to the SEC.

Del Rosario made the confirmation when he was asked by prosecutor Eric Matib and later on by Senator Joel Villanueva if SEC records showed any involvement of the Vice President with GenCorp given that the Vice President listed it as one of her business interests in her 2023, 2024 and 2025 SALNs or during her term as Vice President.
“Wala po siya sa [company records ng] GenCorp,” Del Rosario said.
(Her name is not in GenCorp.)

Senator judge and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian then quizzed Del Rosario as to possible scenarios which would explain the Vice President’s declaration of the firm as one of her business interest even if the company’s SEC submissions does not say so.
“Ano po ang posible na nangyari rito?,” Gatchalian said.
(What possibly happened here?)
Del Rosario then said that possibly, the Vice President could be behind the largest subscriber of GenCorp.

“If GenCorp has a corporate subscriber with a controlling interest…based on its GIS, it has corporate subscriber, JTC Group of Companies, which holds 55% of the company’s equity. If I am to give an example [scenario], maaring ang may-ari ng JTC ay si VP Sara, para magkaroon siya ng control dito sa GenCorp na kung saan hindi mag-aapear ‘yung pangalan niya [sa corporate records].
Del Rosario said that based on SEC records, JTC Group of Companies is represented by a certain Jaime T. Cruz.
“Yun po ang isang scenario; kung talagang siya ay may control ng JTC,” Del Rosario added.
(That is one possible scenario, if she is in control of JTC," Del Rosario added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Should you worry about the Philippines’ P21-trillion debt burden in 2027?
articles.summary: Economists tell Rappler that while the Philippines' debt burden remains manageable for now, its growing size and cost mean keeping it sustainable will depend on the economy growing faster than debt…

blocks.text: Economists tell Rappler that while the Philippines' debt burden remains manageable for now, its growing size and cost mean keeping it sustainable will depend on the economy growing faster than debt despite a weak outlook

items: The Philippine government anticipates its national debt will reach P21.48 trillion by the end of 2027, with current debt at P19.39 trillion as of July 2026.
While the debt is manageable for now, concerns are rising due to high borrowing costs and a weakening economy, with interest payments projected to increase significantly.
To improve the debt-to-GDP ratio, the government aims for economic growth to outpace debt accumulation, but challenges remain due to persistent deficits and low growth forecasts.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine government expects its debt to balloon to P21.48 trillion by the end of 2027, a number that sounds almost inconceivably large to most Filipinos.

National government debt already reached a record P19.39 trillion as of end-July, breaching the P19 trillion mark in June. It is projected to reach P19.77 trillion by end-2026 before rising by another P1.71 trillion next year.

blocks.caption: NATIONAL DEBT. The outstanding debt of the Philippines is projected to hit P21.48 trillion by end-2027. Table from Department of Budget and Management’s Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing 2027 report.

blocks.text: To be clear, the Philippines is not facing an immediate debt crisis, but there are growing reasons to watch the debt more closely, particularly as borrowing remains high while economic growth has weakened.
Economists generally look at debt relative to the size of the economy and at whether the government can continue servicing it without sacrificing essential spending. In particular, they look at:

items: Debt-to-GDP ratio, which compares what the government owes with the size of the economy
Deficit-to-GDP ratio, which measures the gap between government revenues and spending that has to be financed through borrowing
Debt service ratio, which looks at how much of the government’s resources goes toward paying principal and interest

blocks.text: They also watch how much government revenue is being eaten up by interest payments specifically, as well as how much debt is exposed to foreign currencies.

blocks.caption: Should you worry about the Philippines’ P21-trillion debt burden in 2027?

blocks.text: By those measures, the Philippines’ debt burden is elevated and becoming more costly to carry.

The ratio of national government debt to gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to hover around 65% in 2026, before gradually declining to around 63% by 2030 under the government’s fiscal program. The deficit, meanwhile, is projected at 5.4% of GDP this year and 5.1% in 2027, eventually narrowing to 3.5% by 2030.

blocks.caption: FUTURE IMPROVEMENT? Economic managers expect the national debt-to-GDP ratio to improve to around 63% by 2030. Photo from Department of Finance presentation.

blocks.text: There is also the rising cost of servicing that debt. Interest payments are programmed to climb from P950 billion in 2026 to P1.114 trillion in 2027, equivalent to around 15.5% of the proposed P7.2-trillion budget.
Economic managers say they intend to reduce these pressures gradually through fiscal consolidation, with revenues growing faster than spending.
“As revenues grow faster than disbursements, we will see a clear and sustained path towards fiscal consolidation,” Finance Secretary Frederick Go told senators during an August 27 budget hearing.

The rapid buildup doesn’t necessarily mean the government is borrowing more than planned for the full year. Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan said borrowing can be front-loaded, or done earlier in the year to cover upcoming maturities or lock in better rates. Still, “the pace is concerning,” he said, as persistent deficits, new domestic and foreign borrowing, and a weaker peso continue to push the debt stock higher.

blocks.caption: As peso lingers at record-low P62, what does it mean for Filipinos?

blocks.text: Security Bank chief economist Angelo Taningco told Rappler that the Philippines’ debt remains manageable currently, but that “risks are already growing based on larger maturing debt obligations and downbeat GDP outlook.”
Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan is more cautious about the direction.

“The trend of Philippine debt is worrying,” Punongbayan said. “The debt ratio and interest bill are definitely rising, and these tend to crowd out spending on education, health, and other important public goods.”
There are some important buffers.

The finance chief told senators that around 67% of government debt is domestic, around 90% carry fixed interest rates, and 84% has long repayment periods. This makes the country less exposed to abrupt changes in global interest rates or the peso than it would be if most of its debt were foreign-currency denominated or carried floating rates.
Around a third of the debt is still foreign, however, meaning peso depreciation increases the local currency value of those obligations.
The bigger concern is not whether the Philippines can suddenly repay its debts, but whether servicing them can leave little space for other important programs, such as social services.

During House deliberations, budget sponsor Mika Suansing acknowledged that rising interest payments “eating fiscal space,” while ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio likewise pointed out that nearly a quarter of the proposed P7.2-trillion budget will effectively be financed through the deficit.

blocks.caption: Should you worry about the Philippines’ P21-trillion debt burden in 2027?

blocks.text: The government plans around P3.3 trillion in gross borrowing in 2027, although around P1.6 trillion of that will refinance maturing obligations rather than fund new spending.
Bringing the debt burden down will depend heavily on whether the country can improve its economic growth and spend more wisely.

Security Bank chief economist Angelo Taningco told Rappler the debt-to-GDP target remains feasible if growth recovers to at least 5% and consistently outpaces debt accumulation. Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan, however, said the government’s plan becomes much harder amid “meager growth.”

“The way to reduce the debt relative to GDP is to grow the economy much faster, or significantly narrow the government’s deficits,” Punongbayan said. “This requires higher revenues and more disciplined spending.”

“Borrowing for productive investments is defensible, but borrowing for overpriced, substandard, or ghost projects only worsens the debt problem,” he added. – with reports from Paolo Velilla/Rappler.com

articles.title: PPCRV: No irregularities in BARMM election returns count
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Election watchdog Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) has not recorded any discrepancies in its audit of physical election returns (ERs) from the first…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Election watchdog Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) has not recorded any discrepancies in its audit of physical election returns (ERs) from the first Bangsamoro Parliamentary elections, its spokesperson said Monday.

PPCRV spokesperson Ana Singson said they had completed scanning 40.10%, or 2,090, of the 5,212 ERs from the precincts. She also said they were confident they could finish the unofficial parallel count of the voter receipts by Wednesday.

“So far, there are no discrepancies between the transmitted and the scanned physical copies, but as I mentioned a while ago, there are more [ERs] that are not readable,” she told reporters in an interview.
Singson earlier said 11 of the 1,826 ERs they checked last Friday were unreadable. She noted that six more ERs for Monday’s operations could not be scanned properly.
Despite the issue with unreadable ERs, Singson said the PPCRV had not found any other irregularities in its audit.

“Aside from that, we have not found any true irregularities yet, which is good, and we hope it stays that way because people ask us, why do you do this, why do you spend so much time and resources to find one or three or even no discrepancies. Well, the purpose is to find if the elections are clean, honest, accurate, meaningful, peaceful elections,” she added.
She underscored the importance of a manual parallel count to verify the integrity of the electronically transmitted votes and confirm whether the results from the data server match the physical ERs.

Singson also said the PPCRV was receiving more ERs from the final testing and sealing (FTS) than from actual voter receipts. The Commission on Elections (Comelec) conducts FTS using official ballots to ensure that all systems are working accurately for the elections.
Meanwhile, Comelec Chairperson George Erwin Garcia told the Inquirer on Monday that the issue with unreadable ERs was not observed during the FTS.
Garcia added that they would determine whether other copies of the ERs in the same precinct were also unreadable.

Singson said the issue should not have reached the FTS stage, adding that “prior to that, I would think that the machines should have been properly maintained by Miru because those are rented, we didn’t buy them. The maintenance is not on us.” /mcm

articles.title: Weather tracker: Japanese islands brace for Dujuan to become a typhoon again
articles.summary:
Storm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quiet

Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding…

blocks.text: Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back into a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph.

Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands.

Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week.

The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto.

South-west Europe may get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.

articles.title: Kids' repeated online exposure to school violence magnifies fear, confusion --NCMH
articles.summary: Authorities warned the public about the risks associated with young people repeatedly viewing violent online content about school shootings.

blocks.text: Following the latest fatal school shooting incident in Banga, South Cotabato, authorities warned the public about the risks associated with young people repeatedly viewing violent online content about school shootings.

The National Center for Mental Health (NCMH) emphasized on Monday that while social media plays an important role in disseminating information, excessive availability of graphic content on school violence, especially misinformation, can harm students, even those who did not experience the event firsthand.

“Social media can help disseminate information… However, social media can also magnify. Napapalala niya ‘yung fear, ‘yung confusion, and ‘yung emotional distress, especially when young people are repeatedly exposed,” NCMH Medical Center Chief Dr. Noel Reyes said on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon.

(Social media can help disseminate information… However, social media can also magnify things. It worsens fear, confusion, and emotional distress, especially when young people are repeatedly exposed.)
“Lalong-lalo na ngayon ‘yung graphic video, photographs, ‘yung mga opinyon ng iba, speculations, and unverified reports,” he added.
(Especially nowadays with graphic videos, photographs, opinions of others, speculations, and unverified reports.)
Reyes said prolonged consumption of content related to school violence could foster a sense of ongoing threat that may trigger anxiety or intrusive memories in children.

“Even if the child is not present during the incident, repeated exposure may make that a threat. Parang ongoing pa [sa kaniya] ‘yung threat kasi parati siyang exposed doon. They may contribute to anxieties, sleep difficulty, and intrusive memories,” Reyes said.

(Even if a child was not present during the incident, repeated exposure can cause them to perceive it as an active threat. It feels as if the threat is still ongoing because they are constantly exposed to it. This can contribute to anxiety, sleep difficulties, and intrusive memories.)
The NCMH emphasized the importance of close parental monitoring and guidance, especially for children who spend significant time online.
Reyes advised parents to consider setting limits not only on screen time or internet access, but also on the platforms their children visit, engage with, and the content they consume.
He added that adults should be ready and willing to address questions or content that requires parental intervention, which includes explaining right from wrong and reporting harmful online content.
Preventive measures
According to the NCMH, while mental health literacy among Filipinos has noticeably increased, broader mental health promotion needs further reinforcement.

The agency pointed out that student-initiated school violence should not merely be addressed after a crisis occurs, but prevented beforehand by establishing a whole-of-community mental health support system.

“Unang-una po… there should be a mental health promotion for all students. This includes [having] a safe and nurturing school environment, school emotional learning, sustained anti-bullying programs, ‘yung mga responsible digital citizenship po, ‘yung mga parent education and training,” Reyes said.

(First and foremost… there should be mental health promotion for all students. This includes fostering a safe and nurturing school environment, social-emotional learning, sustained anti-bullying programs, responsible digital citizenship, and parent education and training.)
To promote mental health, the NCMH stated it is willing to launch school caravans to help expand mental health awareness and literacy across academic institutions.
Reyes noted that Filipinos are sometimes deterred from seeking help due to the stigma surrounding mental health in the country, which is often tied to shame.

“Sometimes kasi napipigilan ang pag-seek ng intervention because of stigma. Base po sa ating kultura na tinitignan po talaga nating mga kapwa Pilipino na ang karamdaman sa pag-iisip o kaguluhan sa pag-iisip ay senyales po ng kahinaan or kaya nagdudulot po sa kanila ng shame,” Reyes said.
(Sometimes, seeking intervention is hindered by stigma. Culturally, many Filipinos still view mental illness or psychological distress as a sign of weakness, or something that brings shame.)
“Hindi po ganon ang mental illness. Agaran po natin dapat tanggalin ang stigma upang ang intervention ay right time,” he added.
(Mental illness is not like that. We must immediately eliminate this stigma so that intervention occurs at the right time.)
In addition to the early identification of students in need of mental health assistance, the NCMH stated that schools must provide targeted support for these students.
This includes ensuring access to school counselors or caregivers, establishing preventive wellness programs, and maintaining partnerships with mental health institutions or referral centers.

The NCMH encourages individuals who need mental health support to call its 24/7 crisis hotlines (1553 or 0919-057-1553) or avail free online psychosocial support by scheduling sessions at www.ncmhusaptayo.com.
Parents, teachers, and peers are encouraged to closely monitor children and friends for significant physical and emotional behavioral changes that may signal emotional distress.
Emotional and physical red flags in children experiencing distress may include intense fear of school, nightmares, and stress-induced symptoms like headaches, tremors, or cold extremities.

Meanwhile, more severe indicators could include expressions of hopelessness, alcohol abuse, or self-harm, which all signal a critical need for immediate parental and professional intervention. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Toby Tiangco's attempt to reopen plenary debate on House budget denied
articles.summary: An attempt by Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco on Monday to reopen the plenary debate on the budget of the House of Representatives was denied.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:39pm
An attempt by Navotas City Representative Toby Tiangco on Monday to reopen the plenary debate on the budget of the House of Representatives was denied.
During the plenary session of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, Tiangco questioned the changes of the budget hearing of the House from September 24 to September 17.

"Kaya po tayo nagbibigay ng schedule ng budget is para po makapaghanda yung mga members na magtanong. So kung ang budget ng House ay September 24 pa, natural po ang paghahandaan muna ay yung mga September 18, September 21. So mas logical kung doon po humugot," Tiangco said.

(The reason we provide the budget schedule is so that the members can prepare the questions they want to raise. So, if the House budget is scheduled for September 24, naturally, the members would first prepare for the September 18 and September 21 budget hearings. So, it would be more logical to draw from those instead.)
"So I'm asking for a motion for reconsideration to reopen the budget of the House and be presented to the plenary," he added.
However, Deputy Speaker Janette Garin denied Tiangco's motion, saying that Tiangco was unable to vote during the plenary debate of the budget hearing the lower chamber.

"Section 105 of our rules states, 'when a national report or motion is approved, adopted, or lost, a member who voted with the majority may move for its reconsideration on the same or succeeding session day'," Garin said.

"As we have conferred with the Secretary-General, the Honorable Toby Changco was on official travel abroad. Hence, with due courtesy, Hon. Toby Tiangco, your motion for reconsideration is out of order," she added.
The interpellation on the proposed P27.9 billion budget for Congress was terminated on Thursday, September 17.
The budget covers the Senate, House of Representatives, Commission on Appointments, and the House and Senate Electoral Tribunal. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Think Australia would be better off with less migration? The numbers tell a different story
articles.summary:
The population is ageing and we’re having fewer babies. Labor should keep that in mind as the migration debate rages

  • Get our

blocks.text: The intergenerational report lays bare how today’s growing anti-migration rhetoric clashes with a future where we need to attract people from overseas to help grow the economy and pay for our ageing population.
The “replacement” fertility rate is 2.1 children per woman – this is the average number of births to keep the population steady without migration and we’ve been below this level for 50 years.

The fertility rate is about 1.5 now and the IGR projects it will drop to 1.34 over the coming 40 years. This is how Treasury makes the alarming prediction that by the mid-2060s deaths will outnumber births for the first time.

There is no direct plan to reverse the trend for smaller Australian families, and Chalmers has made it clear Labor has no intention of repeating Peter Costello’s baby bonus or the former Liberal treasurer’s free advice on how many babies we should be having.

“When it comes to fertility rates, I do not and will not give people free advice about these very personal decisions that they make about whether to start a family and when to start a family,” the treasurer said on Monday.
Fair enough, but the seventh IGR tells a very familiar story that Australians are, on average, getting older – and this has big implications for the economy and the budget.
It means there is a smaller share of workers paying the taxes to fund the growing burden of paying for things associated with an ageing population, like healthcare and aged care.
Maintaining a healthy migration program has helped – and will help – Australia overcome these structural challenges.

As the IGR says: “Migration contributes to population growth and slows ageing, while supporting a multicultural society and strengthening the economy through skills, innovation and international connections.”
For those who think we would be better off with less migration, Treasury’s analysis provides some evidence that the opposite is true.
The IGR’s “baseline forecast” assumes a long-run net overseas migration (Nom) figure of 235,000 people a year.
This central case predicts real GDP per person – a reasonable proxy for average living standards – to grow from $99,200 in this financial year, to $157,300 in 40 years’ time.
Treasury economists then ran the numbers under a lower population scenario, where Nom was 50,000 a year less, and where the long-run fertility rate was 1.24, instead of 1.34.
Under this scenario, real GDP per person would be $400 lower in 2065-66 than under the baseline.
after newsletter promotion
That’s not much, but it’s working in the wrong direction.
The impacts of lower population growth are more stark when it comes to forecasts of what’s known as the “dependency ratio”.
In 2025-26, there will be 27.4 people aged 65 and over for every 100 working-age Australians. The IGR projects this ratio will soar to 40 by the mid-2060s; with lower migration it reaches 43.
That hits the budget.
The projected underlying cash deficit with lower population growth is 2.4% in 2065-66, instead of 1.8% under the existing assumptions.
Gross debt as a share of GDP is nearly 10 percentage points higher, at 32.2%.
These are the numbers that any responsible government has to keep in mind when trying to navigate its way safely through the shoals of migration politics.

articles.title: DOH debunks myths, shares facts about suicide
articles.summary: The Philippines observes Suicide Prevention Month every September to raise awareness about suicide prevention and help break the stigma surrounding mental health conditions.

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:22pm
The Philippines observes Suicide Prevention Month every September to raise awareness about suicide prevention and help break the stigma surrounding mental health conditions.

The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday conducted the "Mindful Media: Capacity Development on Responsible Reporting and Ethical Portrayal of Suicide" in Quezon City to strengthen responsible and evidence-informed media practices and promote compassionate and ethical reporting on suicide.
Here are some of the myths about suicide debunked by the DOH:
MYTH: Talking about suicide with someone who is suicidal is a bad idea and can be interpreted as encouragement.
FACT: Talking about suicide can help a person explore options and prevent suicide.
MYTH: Someone who is suicidal is determined to die.
FACT: They may be ambivalent about living or dying. Access to support can help prevent suicide.
"We urge them to address the situation and we want them to have access to available support," said Jason Roque, officer-in-charge division chief of the DOH Health Promotion Bureau.
MYTH: Most suicides happen suddenly without warning.
FACT: Most suicides are preceded by warning signs.
Speaking to the media, Roque said there are warning signs that may indicate that a person is at risk of suicide.
These warning signs may be seen in a person's words, feelings and actions.
Words: Expressing hopelessness, wanting to die or asking about suicide methods.
Feelings: Severe sadness, mood swings, unexpected rage and loss of interest.
Actions: Withdrawal from usual activities and isolation.
MYTH: Once someone is suicidal, they will remain suicidal.
FACT: Heightened suicide risk is often short-term and specific to a situation.
"Suicidal thoughts are not permanent. It is short term and specific to a situation," Roque said.
"It's not permanent for an entire life of an individual because because a person can be triggered by different situations in their life," he added.
These situations may include relationship concerns, financial problems, conflict, disasters, violence, abuse and loss.
MYTH: Suicide is an appropriate means of coping with problems.
FACT: Suicide is not a constructive means of coping with problems.
Roque said it is better to talk to family members and peers when dealing with problems.
MYTH: Only people with mental disorders are suicidal.
FACT: Suicidal behavior can indicate deep unhappiness but does not necessarily mean that a person has a mental disorder.
"There are so many things that can lead to deep unhappiness that may trigger a suicide attempt or the act of suicide itself," Roque said.
MYTH: Suicidal behavior is easy to explain.
FACT: Suicide is complex and cannot be explained in simplistic ways.
"It's not easy. It's difficult to discuss because you cannot easily talk about it. Discussing it can feel like you're walking on eggshells," Roque said.
To help avoid the stigma surrounding suicide, the DOH also presented the following terms that the public may use when talking about suicide:

items: Instead of "committed suicide," use "died by suicide" or "dying by suicide."
Instead of "completed suicide" or "successful suicide," use "died by suicide."
Instead of "failed suicide attempt," use "suicide attempt" or "self-directed violence."
Instead of "non-fatal suicide," use "suicide attempt."

articles.title: Alleged 'ghost internet' scheme in DICT under Ombudsman probe
articles.summary: Did taxpayers pay for routers and internet that never worked?

blocks.text: September 21, 2026 | 5:20pm
Composite image shows Ombudsman Boying Remulla (L) photographed in April 2025 when he was still Justice secretary, and DICT Secretary Henry Aguda as seen in June 2025.
Senate PRIB; PNA / Yancy Lim, file

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman is investigating whether the government paid for internet connections that were never delivered and IT systems equipped with substandard or even fake software, in what investigators have dubbed a "ghost internet" scheme.
The fact-finding investigation centers on projects of the Department of Information and Communications Technology, including the government's Free Wi-Fi program.

Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said investigators are examining whether contracted internet sites were actually installed and functioning, whether the government was billed for connectivity that was never delivered, and whether prices for hardware, software and services were inflated.
One potential loophole, Clavano said, is that government inspections may have focused on physical equipment such as machines and routers without adequately checking the software installed in them.

"And there comes the loophole. A contractor can install cheaper, outdated, or even fake software while still charging the government full price for the real thing," Clavano said at a September 18 briefing.
"Because nobody verifies the software after the hardware is approved, the overpricing goes undetected."
Investigators are also looking into who approved, certified or authorized payment for projects that may not have been fully delivered.

"Were the contracted sites actually installed, and are they working? Was the government billed for connectivity and services that were never delivered? Were the prices of hardware, software, and services reasonable or were they inflated?" Clavano said.
Routers but no internet
The investigation also covers allegations that some sites under the government's Free Wi-Fi program had equipment installed but did not actually provide internet access.
"Kaya parang niloloko na lang ho 'yung taumbayan dahil sinasabi na may free internet, free Wi-Fi, 'yun pala naglalagay lang sila ng mga router na wala namang lumalabas na internet," Clavano said.
("So it appears the public is being fooled because they are told there is free internet or free Wi-Fi, when routers are installed but no internet service is actually coming through.")
The Ombudsman's inquiry remains at the fact-finding stage, and no findings of liability have been made.
The DICT said Sunday, September 20 that it has yet to receive formal notice of the investigation but is prepared to provide records, technical information and system data.
"Although no formal notice has been received from the Office of the Ombudsman to date, the DICT proactively welcomes the inquiry," the agency said.
The DICT said Secretary Henry Aguda has ordered tighter monitoring of the Free Wi-Fi program, including technical audits and contractual sanctions for reported inactive or non-performing sites.

The agency also said it upgraded its network monitoring system to provide real-time information on Free Wi-Fi sites and verify whether contractors are delivering the services for which the government is paying.

Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice".
The three suspects are due in court on Monday morning.
Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday.

Published September 21, 2026last updated September 21, 2026
Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

blocks.caption: Plans for a highway toll (Maut) in Germany have so far failed Image: Bernd Wüstneck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.

Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.
Both of them deny the charges made against them.
What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?

The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.

Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.
The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.
But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.
The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.
Jail sentences possible
The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.
If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.

articles.title: Rebel Wilson back in court as The Deb producers sue star over allegedly blocking film
articles.summary:
Hollywood actress appears in NSW supreme court in Sydney for the latest lawsuit over her directorial debut

  • Get our

blocks.text: Hollywood star Rebel Wilson had a “last chance” phone call with her film’s co-producers over a dispute about up-front costs and her $1m fee, a judge has heard.
The Pitch Perfect and Bridesmaids star appeared in the New South Wales supreme court in Sydney on Monday in the latest lawsuit over her directorial debut, a musical comedy named The Deb.
The film’s release was shelved in 2024 after Wilson fell out with co-producers.

Vince Holden, Gregor Cameron and Amanda Ghost claim Wilson and her company, Camp Sugar, breached consumer law concerning misleading conduct and breached various contracts when making allegedly defamatory statements about them to her 11 million Instagram followers in July 2024.
The producers claimed Wilson accused them of inappropriate conduct toward the lead actor in the film, embezzling funds and trying to block its release.
Wilson was accused of preventing the release by undermining negotiations with potential distributors and threatening an injunction against showing the film in Australia.

In a cross-claim, Wilson and Camp Sugar allege Ghost, Cameron and Holden’s involvement in the film was marked by “a troubling pattern of illicit egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct”.
Wilson claimed Ghost broke verbal agreements over writing credits and a soundtrack album deal and Cameron and Holden embezzled $900,000 from a joint venture company set up to make the film.
Wilson sat in the back row of the small courtroom, frequently typing on her phone, as her barrister, Dauid Sibtain SC, questioned one of the film’s producers.
Holden, part of AI Film Production Limited, which brought the lawsuit, was asked about a series of budget and financing emails regarding the 2024 film.
Holden agreed he asked for a “last-chance call” in October 2023 over AI Film’s requests for increased fees and Wilson’s offer to reduce her acting and directing fee to $1m.
Sibtain asked if Wilson had been incredibly upset and angry at AI Film’s proposed $300,000 fee rising to more than $650,000 plus finance costs without consulting her.
“I would not say upset,” Holden said.
“She didn’t like the fees being there.”
After he cut off further money towards the film, Holden told fellow producers: “the clock has stopped ticking and I’m waiting for the boom.”
“AI Film had advanced considerable funds to keep the production on time and we didn’t have a final agreement on fee levels,” he said.
AI Film had planned an “extremely bold investment” toward producing The Deb before securing a share of the rights to the film.
“You accepted that $15m was a lot of money to risk on a first-time director, do you agree?” Sibtain asked.
“Correct, yes,” Holden said.
after newsletter promotion
Holden agreed AI Film was “quite content to risk that money and see where it ended up” and that the risk increased when the budget “subsequently went up to over $20m”.
AI Film company directors claimed these alleged statements breached contracts and Wilson’s obligations as production company director.
That allegedly caused economic loss, a potential film distributor to withdraw an offer and reputational damage to the producers.
Wilson and her company had an initial fee of six per cent of the film’s budget, shared 50-50 with AI Film.
The Deb – eventually released in April 2026 – had multiple estimates for its potential worldwide revenue, starting from a predicted loss of $4.5m if it performed poorly.
If successful, the film could “break even” or make a multimillion-dollar profit, Justice Elisabeth Peden heard.
As a musical comedy with an Australian theme, The Deb’s predicted revenue was based on films Pitch Perfect, Muriel’s Wedding, The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and Strictly Ballroom.
“They were all breakout successes but some of them came out 15 to 30 years ago,” Sibtain said.
“When people went to cinemas, before streaming.”
The hearing continues.
The equity case comes after a blockbuster defamation trial in May involving Wilson and the star of her directorial debut.
Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes claimed she was defamed in four social media posts by Wilson but a judge in July dismissed the case.

articles.title: Sara Duterte declines comment on impeachment trial: I might be cited in contempt
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday declined to give any comment on the ongoing impeachment trial against her, saying she didn"t want to give her lawyers more problems if she is cited for contempt

blocks.text: Published September 21, 2026 5:01pm
Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday declined to give any comment on the ongoing impeachment trial against her, saying she didn’t want to give her lawyers more problems if she is cited for contempt
Duterte balked at making any comment on the proceedings after two prosecutors were issued show-cause orders over comments they made regarding her trial.
“Mako-contempt ako sir, eh, kapag sumagot ako sa impeachment (I might be held in contempt if I talk about the impeachment),” Duterte said in an ambush interview.
“Masyado nang maraming problema ang mga abogado ko. Ayaw ko nang dagdagan yung kanilang problema with the contempt,” she added.
(My lawyers already have too many problems. I don’t want to add to their problems with the contempt.)
Duterte has yet to personally appear before the Senate impeachment court. She is represented by her defense team.
Her trial entered its 27th day this Monday, with the impeachment court tackling Article II, which accuses the Vice President of accumulating unexplained wealth.

The House prosecution panel has finished its presentation on Article I, which alleges misuse of confidential funds, as well as Article IV, which accuses her of making grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and others.
Receptive
Meanwhile, Michael Poa, the spokesperson of Duterte's defense team, said that he is always in constant communication with the vice president regarding statements on the trial.
"Hindi ko naman ide-deny na nagkaroon ng paguusap between myself and the vice president....Very receptive naman po ang ating vice president," he said in a press briefing.
(I won't deny that there were conversations between the Vice President and me.... Our Vice President is actually very receptive.)

"May mga bagay naman kaming napag-usapan na 'Kung sasabihin mo ito, palagay ko this will be covered by sub judice,' at 'Kung sasabihin mo man 'yung ibang bagay, I don't think naman sub judice 'yan.' So may mga ganyan kaming pag-uusap," Poa added.

(There were things we discussed like, 'If you say this, I think this will be covered by sub judice', and 'If you say other things, I don't think that's sub judice.' So we had those kinds of discussions.) –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Babies ‘will face almost twice as much’ extreme fire weather in Europe than great-grandparents
articles.summary:
Children born after 2025 will experience three more years of brutally fire-conducive weather as global heating intensifies

European babies will face almost twice as much extreme fire weather…

blocks.text: European babies will face almost twice as much extreme fire weather as their great-grandparents if climate action does not ramp up quickly, a study has found.

Global heating under current policies will expose a child born in Europe in 2025 to three more years of brutally fire-conducive weather over their lifetime than someone born in 1950, the researchers found.

The number of days with the most severe conditions for fires to burn hotter and spread further will rise fastest in the Mediterranean, where generation Beta, the demographic cohort born from 2025, is to face five more years of lifetime exposure to extreme fire weather than boomers, born in the two decades after the second world war.

The hot, dry and windy conditions that let small fires explode into raging infernos have been exacerbated by one-and-a-half centuries of fossil fuel pollution and the widespread destruction of nature, which has heated the planet by 1.4C. In Europe, which has warmed twice as fast as the global average, the worsening weather has increasingly fuelled monster infernos that overwhelm authorities.

Rosa Pietroiusti, a climate researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel and lead author of the study, said severe fire weather was a “necessary but not sufficient condition” for the kind of extreme fires that ravaged parts of Europe this summer. “The meteorological conditions are an important element of fire risk – the possibility of that fire happening, being super-destructive and difficult to control, and spreading very fast.”

The researchers combined demographic data with outputs from global climate models and tallied the number of days when fire weather was more severe than the worst 5% of days for that region in the reference period from 1985 to 2014. They considered 21 scenarios that resulted in 1.5C to 3.5C of global heating by the end of the century, a spectrum that roughly covers the best- and worst-case scenarios humanity is likely to face.

They found that under current policies, which will result in 2.6C of warming, children born today can expect to experience 84% more exposure to extreme fire weather than those born in 1950. They attributed 86% of the increase to climate change and 14% to people living longer.

If end-of-century warming is limited to 1.5C – a target likely to be crossed in just a few years – children born in 2025 would face 1.3 fewer years of extreme fire weather than under current policies, the study found.
Raúl Cordero, a climate scientist at the University of Groningen, who was not involved in the research, said it highlighted the “inherently intergenerational injustice” of climate breakdown.
after newsletter promotion

“Just one month ago, inhabitants of central Europe experienced fire-weather conditions that their parents or grandparents had never encountered. Unfortunately, these conditions materialised in record-breaking fires in Belgium and western Germany,” said Cordero, whose relatives were among the thousands who fled their homes in Germany in August. “An unstoppable fire engulfing a town? This kind of emergency would have been unthinkable for Germans of older generations.”

In southern Europe, the number of fires and the area burned have declined over decades as authorities have grown better at suppressing them, according to a study Cordero co-authored in July, but in recent years the trend has reversed. As well as hotter and drier weather, aggressive fire suppression – preventing even low-intensity fires – has led to buildups of flammable vegetation that has fuelled ferocious blazes in years when climatological conditions are ripe.

Relentless heatwaves and widespread drought plagued Europe this summer and led to explosive wildfires across France, Spain, Italy and several other countries. Across the EU, the severity of fire weather this year broke records, while the area burned is shaping up to be the third-worst on record.

The EU’s civil protection mechanism was activated nine times as countries scrambled firefighting planes and crews to assist overwhelmed neighbours. In her annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, paid tribute to a Danish firefighter pilot who died with a colleague in Greece last month, and announced plans for the creation of a European firefighting fleet.
“I am so proud of Europe’s response, of our European assets flying across the continent,” said von der Leyen. “But clearly, we need to think bigger and learn faster.”

articles.title: Identifying unclaimed ashes at N.S. funeral home through DNA ‘very challenging,’ says expert
articles.summary: DNA expert Dean Hildebrand says that getting DNA from ashes is very challenging due to the high heat and prolonged duration of cremation. This comes as families in Annapolis Valley struggle to…

image.caption: When East Coast Memorial recently took possession of Serenity Funeral Home in Coldbrook, N.S., the new staff discovered a 'significant number' of cremated remains. The company has been calling families so they can retrieve them. (Angela MacIvor/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

DNA expert Dean Hildebrand says that getting DNA from ashes is very challenging due to the high heat and prolonged duration of cremation. This comes as families in Annapolis Valley struggle to identify buried ashes that aren't who they thought they were.
Heat from cremation destroys all genetic material

While some families in the Annapolis Valley grapple with uncertainty after discovering they may not have buried the actual ashes of their loved ones, an expert in DNA testing says the technology only offers a faint hope of positively identifying the remains.

Several families who used the services of the former Serenity Funeral Home were informed by the home's new owners earlier this month that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones were found in storage.
Michelle Carey had used Serenity when her father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, died in 2018. Hank had specific instructions for his funeral arrangements, including dealing with the funeral home.

Now, having to go through the burial process all over again and being unsure whose remains the family actually buried, she says she’s skeptical that they’ll ever be sure of the identity of the remains.

“Well, my sister and I talked and did a little bit of research and it would be very, very difficult to do any sort of DNA testing,” says Carey. “How do we know for sure that what we're going to get is, in fact, our father's remains this time?”
Dean Hildebrand, who manages the Forensic DNA Laboratory at the British Columbia Institute of Technology, says it’s very challenging to get enough DNA from ashes to make an identification.

items: More stories from Annapolis Valley

blocks.text: “It's not to say that some people or some scientists have reported that you can still find trace amounts of DNA,” he says. “But finding trace amounts of DNA is different from being able to use that [DNA].”
Hildebrand says that DNA is surprisingly robust, noting that labs very often get full DNA profiles from human remains that were in car or building fires, despite the damage done.
But the conditions of a crematorium, 900 C for up to three hours, result in a total breakdown of all organic matter.

items: N.S. families thought they buried their loved ones. Officials are now investigating

blocks.text: "[It’s] kind of a worst-case scenario for isolating,” said Hildebrand.

He says throughout his career he’s dealt with identifying remains of ashes being mixed up involving other funeral homes. But in this case there are a significant number of remains, according to the new owners of Serenity funeral homes, East Coast Memorial.
While the odds of making an identification are low, Hildebrand says he wouldn’t say it’s impossible.
He said that it’s worth testing in case a fragment of bone could yield useful DNA.
“I think it's worth the effort,” he says. “But of course, you have to set expectations.”
Michelle Carey says she was told that the ashes the family buried may contain a small metal disc with an ID number on it, which could lead to identifying the remains.
But the presence of that ID number may be the only way to find out who they originally buried back in 2018.
“I want to believe that what they're telling me is true, that they do in fact have our father's remains,” says Carey. “But it will be very difficult to find out who is the person that was buried.”
The province and the Nova Scotia regulator of funeral directors are investigating.

articles.title: 'Just plain panic': Fears mount as N.B. considers restricting U.S. hunters, anglers
articles.summary: Hunters and anglers from the United States as well as New Brunswick outfitters say they were caught off guard by the province's move to possibly "restrict" hunting and fishing licences in response to…

image.caption: Bradford Burns looks out at his fishing pools from his camp property alongside the Main Southwest Miramichi River. (Shane Fowler/CBC)

blocks.text: Bradford Burns grew up in Friendship, Maine, a town south of Augusta made up of just over 1,000 people. It rests on a peninsula and hosts a public wharf used by dozens of lobster fishers.

That included his grandfather. He’d spend time with him on the boat helping to place bait in lobster traps. But, as he grew up, his taste for fishing brought him inland. First for brook trout. Then he hooked his first salmon.

“There's just a lot of things that scratched a lot of itches for me,” said Burns. “I really got into it, and I really sort of abandoned saltwater fishing after I came here and started making this the focus of my fishing.”
"Here" is New Brunswick. For the last 25 years, Burns has made the six-hour drive from Friendship to Blackville multiple times a year.
This year, he stayed in New Brunswick from mid-June to mid-July, fishing the early salmon run before returning home to his wife, June.
This fall, he’ll spend another five weeks in the province fishing with companions he’s invited from the U.S. and reconnecting with locals.
He loves the wilderness and the people. But mostly he just loves a big fish.
“Every day it's a little different. Some of them pass up the river through the pool," Burns said.
"Those will stay here for a few days, and you'll see them jumping. You'll even get to recognize your particular fish for a few days, and then they're gone.
“It's just interesting to me and exciting and very natural and wild. And so I just like everything about it.”
At 75, Burns is very invested in salmon fishing. He’s bought multiple fishing camps on the shores of the Cains River and the Miramichi.
He owns the rights to Campbells and Keenans fishing pools in front of his fishing camp just outside of Blackville. He owns Doctor's Island in the town that hosts multiple fishing camps.

“I've spent over a million dollars in buying these camps up here and, you know, I don't know if I'll ever get it back,” said Burns, who made his money in the copy business. “But I figured, whatever I spent on it was for my hobby.”
That’s why the idea of not being allowed to obtain a New Brunswick fishing licence is unthinkable.
Hunters on both sides of border react to possible curb on hunting, fishing licences
On Sept. 10, Premier Susan Holt detailed responses to new tariffs from the U.S.

In the aftermath of President Donald Trump imposing new 50 per cent tariffs on select Canadian goods and blocking the import of Canadian alcohol, the province stated it would work to eliminate U.S. goods for government contracts. It would prioritize Canadian goods and work to develop supports for moving away from American markets.
But Holt stated hunting and fishing allowances for Americans could also be targeted.

A following news release from the province states that “the provincial government will continue to pursue additional measures, including undertaking a legislative review to explore giving the minister of natural resources the authority to restrict the issue of fishing and hunting licenses and mining claims based on certain criteria.”

CBC News called and emailed New Brunswick’s Department of Natural Resources communications officer Nick Brown for clarification on what that could mean for U.S. hunters and anglers. CBC News did not receive a response.
But Burns said he believes that could eventually mean hunting and fishing licences will not be available to Americans.

“What good would it do in New Brunswick to take [from] people like me or other people that live along the river; that own property?” asked Burns. “To say, 'Well, you can't come and spend your money here anymore because we're mad at the country, at these officials that have nothing to do with us.'"
Burns described himself as a "Trump Republican." He compared the province's threat of restricting American access to New Brunswick’s fish and wildlife to something his president would do.

“I think, just like Trump has done, is famous for doing, is to come out with these statements that are a little far-fetched, you know, sometimes to get people's attention,” said Burns. “I certainly hope that it's along those lines. I mean that it's not really a serious thought.”
Burns’s sentiment is shared among several New Brunswick outfitters and anglers.
“Putting this industry into that trade war is completely asinine,” said Larry Adair.

He owns Adair's Wilderness Lodge near Poley Mountain. He’s been guiding Americans on hunts since the 70s. Today, he said about 30 per cent of his business comes from the States. But he knows other outfitters, particularly those that cater to bear hunters, where Americans make up nearly 100 per cent of the clientele.
“A lot of our small outfitters, it would devastate them.”
He said his business is only starting to recover from the last time Americans were banned from hunting and fishing the province during the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to Adair, the typical American hunter pays between $3,000 and $5,000 a week to hunt at his outfitting business. That’s on top of paying the province significantly more for a non-resident hunting licence.

New Brunswick’s annual big game harvest reports do not break down sales of hunting licences to Americans. It categorizes them as resident and non-resident licenses. And for the last five years, the number of non-resident licences has been growing.

In 2021, there were 1,954 non-resident moose licences sold. Last year, there were 3,247 sold. In 2021, the province sold 198 deer non-resident licences. In 2025, it sold 363. The report does not tally black bear licences sold.
The cost of a non-resident licences is significantly more for non-residents.

A licence for hunting black bear costs $37 for a New Brunswicker, or $18 if you’re a senior. For non-residents, that same licence costs nearly four times as much — $143, plus a $26.25 application fee.

For a moose licence, New Brunswickers pay $72, or $37 for seniors, plus a $6.30 application fee. Non-residents pay more than seven times as much — $548 for that same licence plus a $26.25 application fee.
For an antlered deer licence, locals pay $34, or $19 for seniors. But non-residents pay five times more for a total of $183.
Adair said a significant portion of those non-resident licences are sold to Americans.
“They have to pay more than your average New Brunswicker or they pay a premium rate,” said Adair.

Those paying Americans have been coming to Upper Oxbow Adventures for more than a century. Co-owner Debbie Norton said her family has guided hunting and fishing guides for five generations now. Her family has lived on the same property alongside the Little Southwest Miramichi River for 203 years.

As an outfitter and the president of the New Brunswick Professional Outfitter Guide Association, she said restricting American hunters from purchasing licences for hunting and fishing would be “crippling.”
“I was a bit astonished and scared,” said Norton about her reaction to hearing about the possibility of restricting American hunters.
Norton said the amount of business the province's outfitters rely on from the States is massive.
"I would have to say that probably over 90 per cent of business in the hunting and fishing outfitting industry in the province comes from Americans," said Norton.
What she’s hearing from the provinces collective of hunting and fishing guides is dire.
“Panic; I think that sums it up the best,” said Norton. “Just plain panic.”
Norton said she and her husband host “hundreds” of Americans each year. She estimated that around 90 per cent of them are repeat customers.
“If somebody is your customer for 40 years, you develop a real friendship with them,” said Norton. “So it sounds a little silly maybe, but sometimes they come just to visit us.”

Norton said she and the association understand that “everything needs to be on the table” regarding Canada’s response to American tariffs. But she argued that American hunting and fishing parties bring in a lot of “new” money to the province, especially in rural areas.

“It's not the hugest industry in the province, but it is a real industry," she said. "It has a tremendous impact, particularly in rural New Brunswick because that's where the industry operates and it will have, should it go forward, it would have a very negative economic outcome for rural New Brunswick in my opinion.”

For Burns, he knows he’ll be able to continue fishing for salmon in the Miramichi and the Cains River throughout the fall until the end of the season. Until then he’s expecting a revolving door for friends coming up for a few days at a time to join him, most of them American. But after Oct. 15, he’ll pack up his fishing gear and head home to Friendship.
What happens over the winter months with New Brunswick’s legislative review will weigh on his mind while he waits to return to his camp for the fishing season to start again.
He said he’ll be at a loss if New Brunswick does move to restrict him from obtaining an angler's licence. It may mark the end of his time coming back to his riverside properties.
“I don't know what I would do,” said Burns. “I guess I'd have to sell it, especially if it was going to be a long-term thing.”
