articles.title: More than a dozen arrested in connection with assassination of Haitian president
articles.summary:
Jovenel Moïse, 53, was shot dead in July 2021 in a killing which sparked chaos in Haiti

Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president…

blocks.text: Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse, according to US officials.
Moïse, 53, was shot dead on 7 July 2021, at his private residence by a hired group of about 20 military-trained Colombian mercenaries. His security detail did not intervene to protect him.
“Today’s multi-location and international arrests underscore the FBI’s continued commitment to bringing all participants in this plot to justice,” FBI special agent Brett Skiles said on Sunday.
The suspects have been taken to Florida to stand trial.
In the same post on X, federal prosecutor Jason Reding Quinones said: “18 transported in military plane from Haiti to face American justice in the southern district of Florida.”
“Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished,” Quinones wrote, adding that 30 suspects have thus far been indicted in the killing.

In May, four men were convicted in a federal court in Miami of charges including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moïse, conspiracy to provide material support and violating the US Neutrality Act to engage in an illicit military operation abroad.
The men face possible sentences of life in prison.

All four were linked to CTU, a private security firm based in Florida, and lured into the plot by the prospect of securing lucrative contracts in the event of Moïse’s ouster, according to federal prosecutors.
Eleven people have already been indicted in connection with the assassination in US courts, which have jurisdiction over plots hatched on American soil.
Five of them have been sentenced to life in prison, including a former Colombian soldier, a former Haitian senator, a Haitian Chilean businessman, a retired Colombian soldier and a Haitian American.
Haiti has descended into deeper chaos since Moïse’s killing, and currently has no president.
It is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016, as well as a referendum on the constitution, on 13 December – if security conditions allow.
Gangs control about 80% of Port-au-Prince, and violent crimes such as kidnappings for ransom, armed robbery and carjackings plague the impoverished nation.
A UN-backed armed force tasked with helping local police combat gangs will not be fully staffed by October as planned, its spokesperson said earlier this month.
Announced by the UN security council last year, the Gang Suppression Force was expected to ramp up between April and October to a planned capacity of 5,500 uniformed personnel and 50 civilian staff.
As of July, it comprised fewer than 1,000 personnel from Chad, Mongolia, Jamaica, Guatemala, El Salvador and Sri Lanka. More recent figures have not been disclosed.

articles.title: AfD makes gains in state elections, but has no government options
articles.summary: Despite making significant gains in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right AfD remains without options to form a state government.

image.caption: AfD co-leader Alice Weidel (m) was jubilant following her party's good showing in state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western PomeraniaImage: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP

blocks.text: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in the elections in northeastern Germany and in the capital, Berlin, but is likely to remain in the opposition in both states.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) scored another election victory on Sunday evening, becoming the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 37.9% of the vote, according to an exit poll by the polling firm infratest-dimap on election night.

That put the far-right party just ahead of the Social Democrats (SPD), whose dramatic comeback in the last few weeks, led by incumbent State Premier Manuela Schwesig, fell just short, with 35.7% of the vote on Sunday evening. The final results may vary as votes are counted.

The AfD was not short of confidence. Even before the first exit poll results were announced, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla told public TV network ARD, "We clearly have a mandate to govern here," before adding that the party would offer coalition talks to all the other parties.
Chrupalla also said he expected Chancellor Friedrich Merz to resign now. "That would truly be a relief for this country," he said.

The AfD also made gains in the Berlin House of Representatives — the state parliament of the German capital — but fell far short of its own expectations on election night. According to infratest-dimap, it took 16.2% of the vote, though it had been polling at 18% only last week.
AfD: 'We are the new people's party!'
With Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) suffering heavy losses in both state elections, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel said she now sees her party as the successor to the CDU.

"We are the new people's party in Germany," Weidel pronounced to public broadcaster ZDF, before criticizing the Christian Democrats for refusing to entertain the possibility of entering into a coalition with AfD: "We are holding talks because we haven't erected any firewalls." But Weidel did not explain what the policy talks with other parties would look like.

After the AfD's triumph in the state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, it has become clear that the party — some of whose members are considered a threat to Germany's constitutional order by German domestic intelligence agencies — is struggling to find political allies.

In that election, the AfD narrowly missed securing an absolute majority of seats in the state parliament and thus cannot elect the state premier on its own. In the struggle to form a governing majority, no party currently appears willing to enter into a coalition with the AfD.
No majorities for the AfD

However, the AfD's leading candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, had made it clear that he would only lead a "stable" AfD government, ruling out a minority government tolerated by representatives from other parties. During the election campaign, he had gone even further, repeatedly stating that he would only serve as state premier in a single-party AfD government.

Since then, it has been unclear exactly what the AfD is aiming for. The AfD's national leadership appears to have a strong interest in seeing form any kind of government. This was underscored by Weidel, who said after the elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania that the AfD could take power "even in a minority government."

Weidel herself is said to have ambitions to succeed Merz as chancellor. She was already her party's chancellor candidate in the last federal election in 2025, and many top AfD officials also see her as the chancellor candidate next time round. A successfully formed AfD state government could potentially give those ambitions a boost.

However, the party's rise has also been accompanied by growing protests. In the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, it was evident that many voters mobilized to keep the AfD's votes in check.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
AfD scandals during the campaign

The party also made several negative headlines during the election campaigns: In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, one AfD candidate had to pull out of the race when it emerged that he was a convicted bank robber. Another candidate withdrew his candidacy for the state parliament when it was revealed he had a DUI conviction and could no longer hold a driver's license.
In Berlin, meanwhile, drugs and Nazi memorabilia were found in the possession of a staff member of the party's lead candidate.

In the past, AfD politicians have repeatedly drawn criticism for making positive allusions to the Nazi era. One AfD European Parliament member posed with his hand on his heart in front of Adolf Hitler's "Führer Bunker" in Berlin, while one Bundestag member described himself as the "friendly face of National Socialism."
The influential AfD state leader in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, was twice fined for using a slogan of the notorious Sturmabteilung (SA), the paramilitary organization of Adolf Hitler's NSDAP party.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Sister of Pakistan's ex-PM Imran Khan arrested
articles.summary: Aleema Khanum is accused of mobilising her brother’s supporters ahead of country-wide protests.

blocks.text: The sister of Pakistan's imprisoned former prime minister, Imran Khan, has been arrested ahead of next week's protests held in his support, his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has said.
Aleema Khanum was detained in the eastern city of Lahore on Sunday afternoon, PTI officials said, calling it an "illegal detention". Her son is demanding her return.

The order for Khanum's arrest, which came from Lahore's deputy commissioner, alleged that she was mobilising Imran Khan's supporters "through social media and public meetings". It added that she will be detained for 30 days.
Khanum is a vocal critic of her brother's detention, regularly speaking to his supporters and the media.
A police official confirmed Khanum's arrest to the BBC. According to the order, she will be taken to Kot Lakhpat jail in Lahore.
Earlier in the day, her family said they had had "no contact or news of her whereabouts".
"We demand the government immediately disclose her whereabouts and ensure her safe return," Khanum's son Shahrez Khan wrote on X.
Many have linked her arrest to the protests that have been organised across the country on 27 September, when demonstrators plan to march to the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.
The arrest order said Khanum had been mobilising people to "create law and order situations" and "raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the Government."
Streets in Islamabad are already lined with shipping containers, ready to safeguard the city's government buildings.
Local media has reported Pakistan's interior minister as saying that the protests harm the country and that the government will do everything they can to stop them.
Khan has been detained since 2023, when he was sentenced to three years in prison for not declaring money earned from selling gifts he had received while in office.
He has faced charges in over 100 cases, ranging from leaking state secrets to selling state gifts - all of which he has decried as politically motivated.
Last year, the cricket star-turned-politician was jailed for 14 years in a land corruption case - the longest sentence he has received.
While in prison, his health has being deteriorating, and last month Khan had to visit a hospital for an examination.

articles.title: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign
articles.summary:
Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels

Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of…

blocks.text: Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.

In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.

Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.

Iran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks.

The outburst of sabre rattling appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attck since the Saudi Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.
The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies.

Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies when he spurned a call by the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help.

The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthis suddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coast overlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia.

On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages.

In a bid to keep the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that it would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, an undertaking that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily.

Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise.
Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.”
The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September.

Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee.

Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators. Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis.

In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.”
Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”.

In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained.

Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance. He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.”

Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone.

articles.title: Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable
articles.summary:
PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy

No international relationship has more power to…

blocks.text: No international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high.

Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink his midterm dreams.

When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle on Nato and Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs.

Starmer’s “keep calm and carry on” strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood.

Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in June signalled he would take a different direction. “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.”

Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.

Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama.

Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trump suggested Burnham was “extremely liberal” (not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”.

The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that he might not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands, and that he would love to see a united Ireland, suggest his displeasure has not abated.

But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shown with the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that he can warm to leftwingers.

On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about the UK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban.
Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes.

It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail.

Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trump told world leaders their countries were “going to hell” over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow.
after newsletter promotion

Burnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US.

But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president.

With Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable.

Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change.
So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him.

articles.title: Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections
articles.summary:
Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin

Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and…

blocks.text: Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party.

Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just over the 5% threshold to enter the state parliament in the coastal region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, its worst-ever state score, which he called a “disaster”.

The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with nearly 38%, more than doubling its previous score.

In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result.
The deeply unpopular Merz has been fighting for his political survival after a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year.
Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch after Saxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routed the CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago.

The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties.

In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy.
Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”.
“Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said.

But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.”

blocks.caption: The AfD’s co-chair, Tino Chrupalla, react as he hears the first results of the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election in Schwerin. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

blocks.text: A jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign.
About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029.
Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs.

If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Poland head into elections next year with nativist parties on the march.
after newsletter promotion

Germany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election.

The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support for Ukraine and carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals.

The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival, Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months.

blocks.caption: Elif Eralp (centre), the candidate for Die Linke in Berlin, reacts to the projected results of the state election. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Merz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support.

A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with only one in 10 Germans saying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked in the former communist east, where the AfD is strongest.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government.

She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it.

A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.

articles.title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of expected first Trump meeting

articles.title: German Chancellor Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in state election
articles.summary: Exit polls show damaging losses for Merz's centre-right CDU party in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

blocks.text: Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party.

In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster".
In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).
Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.
Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours.

According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. However, it is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it.
For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%.
Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.
Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months.

articles.title: 'He could barely paddle anymore': B.C. family rescues bear cub from Okanagan Lake
articles.summary: A B.C. family was boating on Okanagan Lake last weekend when they spotted a baby bear cub struggling to keep its head above water and pulled it onto their boat.

image.caption: The family spotted the cub in the water on Sept. 12, 2026, and brought it back to shore where it ran into the woods. (Submitted by Christina Zamniuk)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A B.C. family was boating on Okanagan Lake last weekend when they spotted a baby bear cub struggling to keep its head above water and pulled it onto their boat.
Family left with concerns around how authorities responded to their calls
Initially, the Zamniuk family wasn’t worried about the cub, but the situation quickly changed.
"All of a sudden, his little nose kept going under the water and he was blowing little bubbles," said Christina Zamniuk.
"He could barely paddle anymore."

She said after her family got the cub, who they named "Boo Boo," on board, it was visibly shivering and shaking from the cold water. The Zamniuks fed the cub some cheese while it warmed up in the sun.
Reporting it
The family immediately called the B.C. Conservation Officer Service (COS) and the B.C. SPCA, who directed them to bring the cub to shore and avoid interacting with it more than necessary.
"Nobody was really much help," said Zamniuk.
Zamniuk explained that once they reached shore in the direction the cub had been swimming, it didn’t want to leave the boat.
"He wanted to stay with us. So, we gave him a little shove and he plopped in the water, he swam to shore and we saw him run off into the woods."
But the COS didn’t come to the scene or provide Zamniuk with any clarity on what could happen to the bear cub next.
"I gave him the address and everything," she said. "They didn’t go."
"They were just so adamant about us not touching the bear because I guess if you have your human scent on them or they get too used to people, then they can’t survive on their own."
Public reminder
The COS confirmed the incident in an email Sunday, and said its officers have not received any more reports of a suspected orphan bear cub in the area.
WildSafeBC, an educational program aimed at preventing conflict with wildlife, said in an email that the outcome was good for both the cub and the people who rescued it.

items: 3rd grizzly in family of 4 killed in B.C.'s West Kootenay
B.C. wildlife rescue says the province is blocking it from saving animals in Prince George region

blocks.text: A spokesperson from the Central Okanagan branch is reminding the public to avoid contact with wildlife and be extremely cautious around wild animals.

The organization said September is a very active time for bears, so encounters may occur more often. It added that if a bear cub is spotted, its mother is likely close by and could become defensive toward people near her cub.
"Black bears are usually good swimmers, and this case is rare that the animal would need human intervention," the email read.
WildSafeBC said the COS should always be the first call if an animal is in distress.

articles.title: Canada, France pledge to work together on space infrastructure, economy
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron have pledged to work together in the areas of space infrastructure, business and economic growth.

image.caption: French President Emmanuel Macron, right, and Prime Minister Mark Carney embrace after delivering remarks in Saint-Pierre, Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French territory 20 kilometres off the southern coast of Newfoundland, on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron have pledged to work together in the areas of space infrastructure, business and economic growth.
Carney and Macron met in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon on Sunday

Speaking to reporters in the French territory of Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon on Sunday, Carney said he and Macron will task their space agencies and defence ministries to develop and share common infrastructure, including space launch systems and ground-based reception facilities.

He said they will also task the regional joint cooperation commission between Atlantic Canada and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon to expand its work in economic growth, energy transition and climate resilience.
Carney said the countries' chambers of commerce are also joining forces to bring their business communities closer together.
The French and Canadian chambers of commerce are expected to sign an agreement in the coming weeks.

The prime minister is in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon Sunday to meet with Macron. The pair shook hands and hugged as Carney stepped off the plane, with several airport workers huddled nearby to take photos and videos of the leaders.
The leaders took park in a working lunch before attending a wreath-laying ceremony at a memorial for the volunteers of Free France.
In December 1941, Free French forces peacefully liberated the archipelago from the control of the Vichy regime, which aided Nazi Germany during the Second World War.

Macron was scheduled to be on the islands, which sit about 20 kilometres off the south coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, for three days over this weekend, before travelling to New York City for the UN General Assembly.
Carney, who will fly to New York on Monday, opted to join Macron for what both countries said is a visit to demonstrate both unity and respect.
Macron's office said Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to have an official visit to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Macron is the first French president to visit in more than a decade.

"In a world characterized by a return to power politics, geopolitical tensions and new dependencies, France and Canada share a common ambition: to work together — and with all countries that share these values — to strengthen their capacity to make decisions and act independently," a spokesperson for Macron's office said in an email.

Alain Di Crescenzo, French Chamber of Commerce and Industry President and CEO, said in a statement that strengthening ties with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce marks a "concrete step in our commitment to turning a historic relationship into real business opportunities."

"Our two economies offer genuine complementarities, and by building on them, we can develop shared value chains in strategic sectors for businesses in both countries," said Di Crescenzo. "The trust that already unites our two countries is an advantage that few commercial partnerships in the world can claim — a strength we can build on without preventing us from exploring other markets at the same time."

Canadian Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Candace Laing said in a statement that the organization has already begun deepening its ties with the French business community, including by leading a trade mission of Canadian business leaders to Paris last June.
"We have many more such engagements planned," she said.
The meeting between Carney and Macron comes amid increased tensions with the United States for both Canada and Europe, and as Canada and the European Union work toward a new and broader alliance.
On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union.

In her state of the union speech to the European Parliament, she said the two sides must "urgently reimagine" their partnership and move beyond a free-trade agreement to bring the relationship to the "highest level possible."
Carney addressed the Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, saying he welcomed von der Leyen's ambitions for Canadian partnership.

Carney said while the name and nature of the new arrangement have yet to be determined, the partnership will go up for debate and a vote in Parliament. He said he's interested in expanding a number of ties, including opportunities for young people, and an integrated market for financial services.

Canada and Europe already have a free trade deal — though it has not been ratified by all EU members — and last year Canada became the only non-European member of the EU's new defence procurement program.

Carney signalled a desire to become closer to Europe immediately after becoming prime minister in March 2025, when he travelled to meet Macron in Paris, and King Charles in London, within days of being sworn in.
On Sunday, he said the partnership between Canada and France is at the heart of its growing relationship with Europe.

articles.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
articles.summary: The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation…

image.caption: Germany's shift to EVs is reducing emissions but eroding fuel tax revenues, raising questions about future transportation fundingImage: DW

blocks.text: "People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW bluntly. "The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway."
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year.
Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered cars in the country.

The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%.
Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall
The boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm in the German government, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes.

Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 euro-cents (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 euro-cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax.
With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club.

The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite."
Energy tax revenue in decline

"If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses.
EU overturns combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year.
In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050.
Pressure to reform road funding

"The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report stated. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, the report added.
In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023.
Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits.
In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act.
That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued.
Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said.
How other countries are responding
Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation.

In the UK, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro-cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids.
Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees.

In Switzerland, meanwhile, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations.

Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls.
Why big automakers are losing China
Are road tolls the answer?
In Germany, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account.
"The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster.
"If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report.
Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.
"If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Trump says his planned triumphal arch will double as a military complex to store ammunition
articles.summary: Trump said the updated plans were at the request of the US military and for national security purposes.

blocks.text: Trump says his planned triumphal arch will double as a military complex to store ammunition
A look at the design plans for Trump's triumphal arch as proposed in April
US President Donald Trump has said his proposed triumphal arch will double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.
In a Sunday morning post, Trump said he is updating the plans at the "strong request" of the US military and for "national security purposes".

The "top grade" military complex and arch will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage", he said.
He did not provide details on construction plans or timing, and it's not clear if he needs further approval for the facility.
Image source, Getty Images

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington DC is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch", without specifying what those cities are.
Construction on Trump's 250-foot arch, planned for a site across the Potomac River from Washington DC just outside the Arlington National Cemetery, was expected to begin this month.

A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure. It will stand 250-feet (76m) from its base to the top of the golden lady statue.
At that height, the structure would dwarf the 99-foot Lincoln Memorial nearby and be half as high as the Washington Monument.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Plans for the arch from earlier this year feature a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top, flanked by two gold eagles.

blocks.text: Plans for the arch from earlier this year feature a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top, flanked by two gold eagles.
The BBC has contacted the Department of Defence for more information on the updated plans.

Trump has pursued a number of construction projects during his second term to revamp the US capital, including a gilded makeover of the Oval Office, constructing a White House ballroom estimated to cost around $400m, paving over the White House Rose Garden, and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
The triumphal arch is one of the biggest projects Trump has set his sights on.

articles.title: Peter Thiel: Power, Palantir, and the antichrist
articles.summary: He was early to back Facebook, early to back Donald Trump, and is one of the world’s richest people. But from his theories on the antichrist and AI to his distinctive politics, Peter Thiel is hard to…

image.caption: Peter Thiel lives in Argentina, but his influence is globalImage: Matias Baglietto/REUTERS

blocks.text: He may not hog the limelight in the same way as Donald Trump, Elon Musk, or many of his other friends and associates, but Peter Thiel has a fair claim to be one of the world's most influential figures — as well as one of its richest.

Born in 1967 in Frankfurt am Main in what was then West Germany, the Thiel family moved to the US when Peter was just a year old. The family also spent six years in South-African occupied Namibia from 1971 to 1977.

Thiel's later rise to prominence came on the back of his tech firms and investments. His first major success was Paypal, a digital payments provider with which Musk was initially involved. Thiel then became the first outside investor in Facebook.
Today he also owns part of Musk's SpaceX, as well as OpenAI, and multiple other companies. Forbes puts his personal wealth at $35.7 billion (€31.1 billion).

But perhaps his most noteworthy company is Palantir. The surveillance, AI, and data-analytics company has won government contracts worth billions to create software for the Pentagon as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The company released a 22-point manifesto in April that critics said bore the imprint of "techno-fascism."
But Thiel could be considered as influential in politics as he is in business, and not just in the US.
Palantir’s AI manifesto sparkes global debate on weapons

Though several European countries, including the UK, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Spain are starting to reevaluate or end their governmental and military links with Palantir due to security concerns, the company is deeply embedded in security systems across the globe.

Thiel himself has recently moved to Argentina, where he has reportedly held talks with the country's right-wing president, Javier Milei, as the government proposes a series of regulations that include incentives for foreign companies and targets investments in AI data centers.
Early Trump support paid off

Thiel was an early backer, and later advisor, of Donald Trump, donating $1.25 million to Trump's 2016 election campaign and speaking at the Republican National Convention in the same year, at a time when Silicon Valley was broadly considered to be Democrat-leaning. Bar a hiatus between 2023 and 2025, he has been a generous donor to Republican campaigns and figures, including Vice President JD Vance.
Thiel's own political beliefs are not easy to pin down. He's been described as a libertarian nationalist and consistently expressed the belief that "technology is the alternative to politics."
He also shows a distrust of authorities, regulation, and liberal elites. This is partly born of a frustration with what Thiel considers inefficient decision-making by elected officials and voters.

"It's bordering on fascism," Max Chafkin, who wrote a 2021 biography of Thiel, told Time magazine. "He talks about how companies are better run than governments because they have a single decision-maker — a dictator, basically. He is hostile to the idea of democracy. That's pretty scary when you consider the role the companies that he's been involved in play."

blocks.caption: Thiel backed Donald Trump's first run for president. The two are seen here in December 2016, shortly after Trump won the electionImage: Albin Lohr-Jones/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: These beliefs seemed to start to rise to the surface during his time at Stanford University in California. Thiel railed against the prevailing liberal campus ideology and founded the Stanford Review, a publication to express those contrary beliefs, something that would echo his current disdain for beliefs labeled as "woke."
Christianity, the antichrist, and AI

Thiel was raised in a strongly Christian household, and there is little doubt that his religion has colored his life and career. Thiel recently described himself as a "small 'o' orthodox Christian," something which seems to influence his conservative politics. His homosexuality, and marriage to American financier Matt Danzeisen, seem to many go against that grain. But paradox is not unusual for Thiel.

More recently, he has become preoccupied with the concept of the antichrist, touring with a series of lectures all over the world during the last few years. Rather than the figure depicted in the Bible, Thiel sees this as someone, or some group, who will deliver the apocalypse "by playing on our fears of technology and seducing us into decadence with the antichrist's slogan: Peace and safety."

Among those who have been, somewhat vaguely, cast in the role of soldiers of the antichrist have been environmental activist Greta Thunberg, whom he sees as a "Luddite who wants to stop all science," or governments that seek to regulate AI. He accused Pope Leo XIV of "working for the Chinese communists" in July after the pontiff warned about the "risk of dehumanization" by AI.
Despite his deep association with tech, Thiel also benefits from his relationships with powerful people, Musk, Trump, and Vance among them.

"I've built some great friendships over the years with people I've worked with," Thiel told the Washington Post in 2014. "And I think that's a really important part of what enables one to be successful in the long run in our society."
Inside Peter Thiel's secretive elite Dialog club
Using Vance to future-proof his interests?

Many observers think that Thiel may be using his relationship with Vance to help protect himself and his business interests in the future, with the vice presidentconsidered the most likely Republican to succeed Trump.

The pair met back in 2011 when Thiel gave a talk at Yale Law School. Vance, whose religious beliefs and politics have since shifted, wrote in Christian magazine The Lamp that Thiel "defied the social template I had constructed — that dumb people were Christians and smart ones atheists."

Thiel then reportedly became a mentor figure for Vance, before smoothing the relationship between Vance and Trump as Vance U-turned from previous opposition to the president to join his 2024 ticket. Most notably though, Thiel donated $15 million to Vance's Senate campaign in 2022, the largest amount ever donated to a single US Senate candidate.

The recent calls to slow the pace of AI, made in part by CEOs in similar positions to Thiel, may end up having an impact on Thiel's business interests. But his distinct character and connections have so far kept him a step ahead.
Edited by Carla Bleiker

blocks.text: Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the ⁠UN, ending a ⁠bid ​that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.
Bachelet, 74, announced ⁠her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the ⁠same determination as always, my international work.”

The two-time Chilean ​president and former ‌UN human ‌rights chief had positioned her campaign around defending multilateralism and ‌international law at a time when she said both were under sustained pressure.

Bachelet’s exit leaves seven candidates in the race to succeed the secretary general, António Guterres, who will conclude his second five-year term on ‌31 December. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the contest.
Her ​withdrawal comes after a third informal straw poll, held on Friday, showed her support had all but collapsed. That same poll put Costa ⁠Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan in the lead.

The UN security ​council ​will formally recommend ​a single candidate to the 193-member general ​assembly for election. ‌The assembly’s ​approval ​has long been seen as a formality once the council reaches consensus.

articles.title: 'Agent Layla': Sex assault victim turned secret agent brings her abuser to justice
articles.summary: A new CBC Podcast tells how Vienna Luke, the victim of a historic sexual assault, went undercover as an RCMP agent to record a confession from the family member who assaulted her years earlier.

image.caption: With the support of her sister Shawnessy Luke(left), Vienna Luke became a police agent in her own case. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.
On a Friday morning in 2021, just a couple of days before Halloween, Vienna Luke zipped up an oversized puffer jacket with a big hood, and put on sunglasses to hide her face.
In a SUV outside her home, plainclothes RCMP officers waited to whisk her away on a secret mission — a face-to-face meeting with the man responsible for the worst night of her life.

Luke, a fitness instructor and mother of two children, was the key undercover agent in an RCMP operation that — if successful — could lead to the rarest of outcomes: a criminal conviction in a sexual assault that that had occurred 14 years earlier.
If Luke failed, her case and the truth about what had happened that night would almost surely be lost to time.
The police referred to Luke using a code name: Agent Layla.
CBC has obtained the surreptitious recording of that mission. It shows an extremely rare instance of RCMP turning the victim into an agent in her own case.
The RCMP sergeant who led the investigation say it’s an approach that is almost never tried — especially in sexual assault cases.
"For the victim to have the strength, and the investigative team [to have the] determination[...] is almost unheard of," said Sgt. Joëlle LaChance.

Facing the man who assaulted her, her estranged brother-in-law, "Agent Layla" presses him for answers over the course of 70 minutes. Luke ultimately elicits a confession that surpassed even the highest hopes of the RCMP team gathered in a nearby hotel room listening in over a wire. The breakthrough was so moving that it brought tears to a hardened undercover officer accustomed to working with drug dealers and murderers.
"She literally took her life back in her hands," said one of the officers from the undercover unit, working with LaChance.
"There wasn’t a dry eye in that room," said LaChance.

That recording — along with interviews from Luke, her middle sister Shawnessy Luke, and the police officers involved in the sting — is part of a new four-part CBC podcast called Personally: Agent Layla.

The podcast details how Luke managed to get the truth, put the man who assaulted her behind bars, and begin to heal from an incident that left her traumatized, detached from her own body, and at odds with members of her family who at times failed to take her side.
A night with only one memory

At 20 years old, Luke was living at home with her family in the Vancouver suburbs after attending a Bible school overseas. Her life had been sheltered; she says she had never been kissed, or even held hands with a man.

While she contemplated her future, she decided to move in with her eldest sister, brother-in-law and their sons in the small B.C. town of Fort St. John — a 14-hour drive north from where she was raised.

Her brother-in-law, Justin Sewell, was a respected veterinarian who was active in a local Christian church. Sewell was 11 years older than her and he had been a trusted member of the family since Luke was a child.
During a week when Luke's sister and nephews were out of town, Sewell proposed a plan. He suggested she get drunk for the first time at home with him, in what he described as a "safe place."
Luke says she had heard of another Christian girl who had done something similar to experiment for the first time with drinking, so she went along with his idea.
WARNING: This story contains graphic details about sexual abuse.
According to testimony presented in court and extensive interviews conducted by the CBC, Luke only sipped the cocktails he made — one of them a Kahlua-based "Brown Cow."

As she and Sewell danced to country music in the living room, Luke remembers her legs buckling. As the world went black, she felt nauseous and thought to herself that drinking alcohol didn’t seem so fun after all.
Aloud, she spoke a phrase that only drives home how naive she was to what was about to happen.
"I just love Jesus," she said. "I just love Jesus. And then I was out."

For Luke, everything about the rest of that night is blank, except for one memory that would both torment her and propel her to seek accountability in the almost two decades to come: a brief moment when she says she awoke mostly naked in her bed.
"I was looking at myself, from above, to my brother-in-law taking off my underwear," she said.
'We gotta tell mom and dad'

In the aftermath of that horrible evening, Luke says she tried to "shelve" what happened. For months, she fought what she described as a war between her body that remembered, and her brain trying to forget.

She moved back home to her parents’ home near Vancouver and didn’t come face-to-face with Sewell again until half-a-year later at Christmas when the entire family went to Florida for a cruise. But when they said their goodbyes at the airport, her middle sister, Shawnessy Luke, noticed something was off.
"I remember it like it was yesterday," Shawnessy Luke said. "The way he hugged her. And I think that’s strange. That’s prolonged. And I knew something was going on."

Shawnessy Luke describes herself as a person with great intuition and "like a dog with a bone." She waited until she and Vienna Luke got back to their parent’s home to ask questions. She was doing her laundry in the family’s narrow utility room when she insisted that her sister explain.
"She definitely pulled it out of me," said Vienna Luke. "I did not volunteer."

Vienna Luke told her sister what happened in the days leading up to the drinking game, facts that were accepted in court: How Sewell had held her hand, how he called her up from her basement bedroom to watch a lightning storm and then massaged her back, and how he told her he loved her.
Then she shared how Sewell proposed she get drunk, and how she couldn’t remember much more than that.

"In my moral compass brain, the minute I heard those things, I was like, I don’t need to know anymore, I believe you," said Shawnessy Luke. "We’ve got to tell someone about this because [...] whatever happened to you [...] was wrong."
Shawnessy Luke says she insisted they tell their mom and dad.

The night in question had happened in June 2007, about 10 years before the #MeToo social movement. As Vienna Luke told her parents about Sewell holding her hand and massaging her back, she stopped short of sharing the most damning memory of all — that she woke up to Sewell removing her underwear. She felt like her parents didn’t know how to handle what she was saying, and didn't have the vocabulary at the time to talk about sexual assault.
"I knew that I couldn’t share more," she said.
Her father called Sewell right away. She didn’t overhear their conversation, but she recalls her father handed her the phone and she found herself suddenly on the line with Sewell.

Vienna Luke pleaded with Sewell to tell his wife what had happened, hoping her oldest sister would take her side. She still doesn’t know if that happened, only that her oldest sister has continued to stand by her husband and is still married to him today.

Her parents declined to be interviewed for this story. In a victim impact statement filed in court, they wrote: "Our effort to uncover the full story was unsuccessful. Lacking information and clarity, we had no path forward. We felt uneasy about what we knew, but did not pursue this matter further."
Years of numbing

In the years that followed, the Luke family struggled with the divide created by that night: Vienna’s oldest sister and Sewell on one side, Shawnessy and Vienna Luke on the other, and their parents trying to walk a line between all three of their daughters.
"It was easier to take Justin for his word," Vienna Luke said. "He was the one that knew what happened. He got to write the story."

With no clarity about what had actually happened and that one horrific memory of him removing her underwear replaying in her head, Luke says she spent years feeling like a robot trying to numb her pain.
She also moved out of her parent’s house and moved to Vancouver, got a job, and met a man who she credits for showing her how to love herself again.
When they started a family, Luke says something inside her started to shift. She knew she’d have to tell her children the truth someday, and something about birth reconnected her to her body.
"My body wasn’t just laboring," she wrote in her journal. "[It was] waking up."
Twelve years after the assault, and weeks after she delivered her second child, Luke called up her sister Shawnessy.
"Hey, I’m ready to deal with this," she said.
So the two sisters made a list.
The sister detectives
Together, they wrote down all the names of people they suspected had soured on Sewell after he had disclosed to his wife and friends two extramarital affairs five years earlier.
Shawnessy Luke's first call was to one of those ex-lovers, a female veterinarian who had worked at Sewell's clinic.
In a recording of that phone call shared with CBC and in court testimony, the woman said she and Sewell were discussing previous sexual experiences when he said something shocking.

"So what he told me was that he put ketamine in [Vienna’s] drinks," the ex-lover revealed during a phone call Shawnessy Luke recorded. "But he didn’t know how much was enough to like, make her forget."
The sisters say this new information validated a hunch they had come to believe: that Vienna Luke had been drugged.
It also gave her a little piece of evidence to march into the Vancouver Police Department and report.
'I do my job for the victims'

Vienna Luke's file was transferred up to the small RCMP detachment in Fort St. John. Against all odds, it landed on the desk of Sgt. Joëlle LaChance, a female officer with a special commitment to cases that many officers would simply dismiss as too hard and too old.
"My whole life I have been a champion for the underdog," she said. "Being able to stand up for the victim … it's why I do my job."

LaChance said she knew Sewell — with his stellar reputation in the community, had a lot to lose. So instead of going directly to the veterinarian to question him, she called on other RCMP units for help, including the undercover unit.
Together, they hatched a plan.

Court records show Sewell had emailed Vienna Luke several times in the years since the night of the drinking game, asking her to accept that he had changed and hoping that the extended family could be together again.

Luke showed the police those emails. Together, they crafted back emails that suggested there could be a possibility for family reconciliation, but first Luke would need the whole truth and they’d have to meet face-to-face.
They pitched Sewell on a plan to fly to Vancouver to meet Luke.
Unbeknownst to Sewell, Luke would be prepared.

For weeks, she trained, preparing to grill him for the facts. She spent a couple of days in a hotel room, sitting across from an undercover RCMP officer who role played with her. The officer worked to get her comfortable asking tough, direct questions, using words like "vagina" and "ejaculate" — specific terms that would be necessary for charges to be laid.
"This isn’t a trained hitman," the undercover officer said. "She’s very polite, very soft-spoken. And I knew that was exactly the opposite of what we were going to need to do."

On the day of the sting at Vancouver airport, everyone involved held their breath. RCMP had laid the groundwork, but as soon as the tape started recording and Sewell walked in, it would be entirely up to Luke to get the truth.
For the plan to work, Luke would need to be both victim and hero. The RCMP believed it was the best chance at bringing charges. Luke knew it was her only chance to get answers.
"You think I'm exactly the same," Luke remembered thinking. "You think I'm gonna play your same little game, but we've got a new game and I'm writing it."
An extraordinary encounter – and as much truth as she’ll ever get
In the recording, Sewell sits down across from Luke and quickly tries to take control. He claims pornography and a culture that objectifies women is part of why he assaulted her that night.
"Okay, but you’re not actually telling me what happened," Luke replies. "Let’s get back to the night and what actually … happened."
The undercover officer who had spent time coaching Luke for this moment felt proud.
"Take control of that conversation," he said in an interview while listening back to the recording. "Don’t just accept a two-minute fluffy bullshit answer."
Luke persists, peppering Sewell with questions seeking specific details, seemingly undeterred by the fact she’s learning this information about the worst night of her life for the first time.

On tape, Sewell confesses to drugging her, removing her clothing, masturbating and ejaculating twice on her body, and taking 30 photos, including ones where he is spooning her naked body and one where his penis is near her face.
As Luke prepares to wrap up, she lobs an open ended question.
"Is there anything that I’m not asking?" Luke said.
"No reason for me to disclose this. But I took pictures of you at other times," Sewell replied.
His response allowed the RCMP to recommend another charge, this one for voyeurism.
A rare conviction in a historic sexual assault
In the morning of April 26, 2022, Fort St. John RCMP arrested Sewell as he left his home for work.

Sewell pleaded guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism — one for the photos he took of her the night he assaulted her and one for times he had watched her through her bedroom window. Crown agreed to stay a charge of administering a drug with intent to commit a sexual assault.
In the courtroom, Luke’s mother, father, and Sewell’s supporters listened to the recording from the airport.
A provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to house arrest. Crown appealed and the Court of Appeal judges determined the lower court judge had overstated the mitigating fact of Sewell’s confession.
They issued a sentence of 33 months less a day in prison for his crimes.
Luke asked the court to remove the publication ban on her name — something that is standard in cases of sexual assault to protect the victim’s identity.
As she began to tell friends and acquaintances her whole story, that she was the unnamed victim, she says she realized how important it was to her that she could also say she was the secret agent.
"It took this … experiment of the police saying, 'Hey, how about you go undercover as yourself' for me to realize, whoa, look at the advocate I can be for myself," she said.
"I was Agent Layla. That's me."
The CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla is available wherever you get your podcasts.

If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​

articles.title: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like much of the country, it's not so simple
articles.summary: Canada is spending billions to expand passenger rail after decades of decline, but torn-up tracks, lost corridors and a surviving network built around freight means communities trying to bring trains…

image.caption: The former Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops sit on 3.2 hectares of former railway lands in St. Thomas, Ont. Built in 1913, the building is now home to the Elgin County Railway Museum, but is closed to the public because of structural concerns. (Patrick Morrell/CBC News)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Canada is spending billions to expand passenger rail after decades of decline, but torn-up tracks, lost corridors and a surviving network built around freight means communities trying to bring trains back face a very different railway than the one they lost.
St. Thomas, Ont., is a vivid example of the obstacles facing communities across Canada
What happened to Canada's 'Railway City?'
To an outsider, the 3.2-hectare sea of grass surrounding the Elgin County Railway Museum in the heart of St. Thomas, Ont., might look like an urban park. That's not what Wil Zufelt sees.
To him, it's an enormous open wound.
"You say green space," he said. "We're actually sitting in the middle of a brownfield site that was left behind from the railroads."

Built in 1913, the hulking red-brick building was once the Michigan Central Railway Locomotive Shops, where locomotives were maintained and overhauled by a staff of 400 workers. It's one of three survivors of a sprawling railway complex that once had 112 buildings.
The old building is now a museum, but it can't welcome visitors. It's literally crumbling. The city engineer ordered it closed after finding its walls were bowing and its ceiling was unsafe.
'Pay attention to what we're losing'
"People need to wake up," Zufelt said. "Pay attention to what we're losing."
Zufelt heads Railworks, the organization behind three of St. Thomas's surviving railway landmarks. He's launching a campaign to raise $8 million to save and restore the former locomotive shops.
The goal is to turn the old locomotive shops into not just a museum, but an active gathering place at the centre of a redeveloped downtown.

"I want it to be more than alive. I want it to be the centre of St. Thomas," he said. "That's what success is, is putting a heartbeat back in the core and then you have your arteries and everything pumps out from the middle."

By 1914, eight railways converged on St. Thomas, bringing more than 100 trains through the southwestern Ontario city every day. Its location made it a major hub for American rail traffic between Detroit and Buffalo and between New York and Chicago. The cross-border connection was so important, at one point, St. Thomas even had a U.S. consulate.
Today, the community that calls itself the "Railway City" has no rail connection at all.
Tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere

The railways are long gone, but their remains are scattered across the city — empty lots filled with rubble from where railway buildings once stood, abandoned shunting yards, railway spikes that turn up like seashells on a beach and tracks that snake everywhere and nowhere.
The old London to Port Stanley Railway runs past a restored station in St. Thomas before it abruptly ends — disappearing into the grass of a residential neighbourhood.

The missing connection was the subject of a 1990 federal transport order requiring CN to replace the missing diamond at its own expense once the line reached CN tracks. But the physical connection was never completed.
Today, part of the former route is blocked by a parking lot enclosed by a fence.
The Canadian Transport Agency told CBC News the order remains in effect and CN's obligation would still apply if the physical connection were made.
CN did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.
What St. Thomas tells us about Canada's railways

St. Thomas is an unusually stark example of what happened in communities across Canada as the railway era receded, according to Thomas Blampied, a historian who studied Canada's railway history at the University of Toronto.
"Cars started to eat away at passenger revenue from railways and trucks started to take some of the freight traffic," he said.
As passengers moved to cars and freight moved to trucks, railways abandoned increasingly unprofitable routes. They didn't simply stop running trains. Much of the infrastructure was removed with them.
"Do we keep the infrastructure — so the track, all the signals, all the crossing warnings — do we keep it all intact?" Blampied said. "Increasingly, the answer was no."
In some cases, the rails were sold for scrap, in many cases, he said, "it made economic sense to completely withdraw."
But even where the railway lines survived, the network changed.
Canada looks to bring passenger rail back

Anthony Perl, a transportation policy expert at Simon Fraser University, said railways removed passing tracks and other infrastructure once passenger trains disappeared, reshaping the network around the needs of freight.

"We had a great streamlining, or right-sizing, or value engineering, pick your term — of the national rail infrastructure in Canada as passenger trains went away," Perl said. "To optimize it for long, slow freight trains."
He said that matters now because Canada is trying to put passenger trains back on a network that, in many places, was either removed or rebuilt for another purpose.

In Ontario, the province is preparing to restore Northlander passenger service between Toronto and northeastern Ontario, more than a decade after it was cancelled. The federal government meanwhile, is developing Alto, a new high-speed passenger railway between Toronto and Quebec City that would run largely on its own tracks.
Other communities are pushing for passenger rail to return, including on Vancouver Island, in Alberta between Calgary and Banff and in Cape Breton.
The power of owning the tracks
But Canada's railways have something airlines and trucking companies don't: control over the infrastructure they use.

"No one is going to build an alternative set of rails across this country under any circumstances," Perl said. "That's why they make the call on whether to put in or take out tracks in particular places."
In St. Thomas, CN has yet to restore the missing connection between London and Port Stanley.

"Even when the Canadian Transportation Agency orders them to do something they don't want to do," he said, "it can take quite a while, if ever, that they will go along with it because they have the ownership of that infrastructure."
Perl argues that kind of power has deep roots in the railway business and points to language the industry has given us.
"To 'railroad someone' is to take advantage and treat someone unfairly or unjustly," he said. "You don't see that with too many other industries."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Colin Butler is based in London, Ont., where he reports for Ontario and national audiences. He covers investigative, science, public policy and government accountability with a particular interest in using public records to uncover hidden stories.
